tradition.name: Future ambient
tradition.lineage: A provisional electronic ambient grouping whose representative producers combine synthesis with manipulated everyday sounds and rhythmic sample construction. J.Views documents this approach in contemporary studio work. The candidate models its articulated, sample-based side; exact scope and artist membership require direct Every Noise inspection before publication. Recording and component choices are authored, not universal genre facts.

extras.description: This candidate treats electronic texture and sampling as a composed production language. J.Views demonstrates transforming ordinary objects, vintage synthesizers and drum machines into beats; his 401 Days interview describes preserving raw performances while editing and combining them digitally. The selected ensemble supports those methods without declaring a fixed tempo, dance rhythm or required vintage device for every artist.
exemplars: J.Views — sampling and beat-production studio demonstration (2020)

tradition.name: Indian ambient
tradition.lineage: Ambient work combining Indian classical melodic instruments and contemporary electronic production also operates across the diaspora. The selected sitar-led branch follows Al Gromer Khan’s documented Vilayat Khani training and sitar/synth recordings. This grouping does not imply a single religion, an exclusively Indian production location or one compulsory raga. Exact tuning, construction and recording settings below are authored models.

extras.description: The selected palette places ornamented sitar melody against sustained synthesizer accompaniment. Sitar Secrets documents both straight raga pieces and electronic combinations, with tabla appearing on some tracks. This default represents a spacious, percussion-free branch, rather than prescribing the complete alap–jod–jhala–gat sequence or treating all Indian ambient music as traditional concert performance.
exemplars: Prem Joshua & Manish Vyas — Water Down the Ganges (2002)

tradition.name: J-ambient
tradition.lineage: A provisional broad Japanese ambient grouping spanning electronic environmental composition and later studio electroacoustic work. Hiroshi Yoshimura’s GREEN documents a Tokyo home-studio FM approach; Eiko Ishibashi’s For McCoy documents a later collage practice with synthesizers, field recordings and acoustic collaborators. This proposed scope needs Every Noise membership confirmation. The default is an authored electronic subset, not a reconstruction of either album.

extras.description: The selected electronic subset uses harmonic FM layers and edited recorded sound. Its historical reference is Yoshimura’s unhurried GREEN; the original Japanese mix omitted nature effects later added for a US edition. Ishibashi’s later studio work brings together musique concrète, synthetic layers and recurring acoustic fragments. Neither traditional Japanese instruments nor environmental recordings are compulsory across these examples.

tradition.name: Nordic ambient
tradition.lineage: A provisional regional grouping of ambient practice from Nordic countries. The selected Biosphere branch uses electronic layers and sampled environments rather than an inherited folk ensemble. The documented Tromsø artist profile provides a practice anchor; regional affiliation does not establish a universal icy timbre, national tuning or compulsory ritual setting. Exact Every Noise membership and the wider grouping remain pending.

extras.description: Biosphere’s Wireless documents an immersive live electronic set, integrating natural and science-fiction samples with synthetic material; its credits include field samples and a trumpet contribution. The default selects the synthesizer/sample core and leaves the optional trumpet out. It represents one evidenced production branch rather than making landscape, weather or traditional Nordic instruments mandatory musical features.

tradition.name: Organic ambient
tradition.lineage: An ambient production approach that develops slowly changing, interwoven sound through recording, synthesis and processing. Projekt explicitly classifies Jeff Greinke’s Oceanic as organic ambient, while contemporary label accounts also include acoustic instruments and environmental recordings. The term does not require an acoustic ensemble: Greinke describes Oceanic as entirely sample- and synth-based. The default selects that electronic branch.

extras.description: Layered sources are transformed into evolving timbres and spatial motion. Greinke’s Oceanic uses manipulated samples and synthesizers without additional players; other contemporary label examples integrate field recordings and acoustic textures. The default therefore uses the documented electronic core rather than assuming handpan, strings or flute are mandatory. Nature-oriented ambience is represented by Steve Roach’s processed Australian outdoor recordings in Atmosphere for Dreaming.
